value.overview: The Northern Jacana (Jacana spinosa) is a distinctive wetland bird of Mexico and Central America. It walks across floating leaves and other shallow-water vegetation using exceptionally long toes and claws that spread its weight. Adults have dark heads and underparts, a rich chestnut back, yellow wing markings, and a yellow bill with a blue frontal shield. The species is well known for its unusual breeding system, in which males incubate eggs and care for young.
value.classification: The Northern Jacana belongs to the family Jacanidae, a small group of tropical wetland birds specialized for walking on floating vegetation. Its scientific name is Jacana spinosa.
value.identification: This medium-sized wader has a blackish head, neck, breast, and belly, contrasting with a warm chestnut back and wings. Bright yellow patches are visible in the wings during flight. The bill is yellow, and the forehead has a blue frontal shield. Its most distinctive feature is its very long toes and claws. Juveniles are browner and less sharply marked. It often walks deliberately across lily pads, water lettuce, and other floating plants.
value.rangeHabitat: The Northern Jacana occurs from Mexico through Central America to western Panama, including Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident wetland bird, recorded mainly in lowland areas and in suitable sites on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, although local abundance varies and some areas have relatively few records. It inhabits shallow freshwater marshes, ponds, quiet lake margins, canals, flooded pastures, rice fields, and slow-moving waters with abundant floating vegetation.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica and across most of its range. It is not a long-distance migrant, but may make local or seasonal movements when water levels and wetland conditions change.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place on shallow wetlands with floating vegetation. The species has a polyandrous system: females may mate with several males, while males usually build or arrange the nest, incubate the eggs, and care for the young. Nests are shallow platforms made from aquatic plants and are often placed on floating leaves or low vegetation. Clutches commonly contain four dark-marked eggs. Chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and can swim and forage under parental supervision.
value.dietFeeding: The Northern Jacana feeds mainly on aquatic and terrestrial insects, insect larvae, spiders, and other small invertebrates gathered from floating plants, mud, and shallow water. It also eats seeds and other plant material and may take small fish or other tiny aquatic animals. Its long toes allow it to search across floating vegetation without sinking, while its bill probes leaves and surface debris.
value.behavior: This species usually forages alone or in pairs, walking across floating plants with a slow, high-stepping gait. It swims when necessary and may fly between patches of suitable vegetation with its yellow wing markings conspicuous. Northern Jacanas can be territorial and give sharp calls when disturbed. Females are larger and may defend territories containing several males. Males provide most incubation and parental care, including protecting and guiding the mobile chicks.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable overall, although numbers may vary locally with wetland conditions and habitat changes.
